analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to count workers' previous coverage against preexisting-condition waiting periods.
analysis.headline: The bill won 47 bipartisan cosponsors after its introduction in 1995 but never received a committee vote and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers change jobs, new employer health plans can refuse to pay for treatment of conditions they already had, often for months or years. This bill would force employer-provided group health plans to credit a worker's time covered under a previous plan against any such preexisting-condition waiting period, as long as the worker had no gap in coverage longer than 60 days. It would also bar plans from setting eligibility, enrollment, or contribution rules for these workers based on their health status, medical history, or disability.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with health conditions who change or lose jobs. Instead of restarting a waiting period for coverage of their existing conditions at each new employer, their months of prior coverage would count toward it. People who had been enrolled in a plan would also be protected from being turned away or charged more because of their medical history, claims experience, or disability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with health conditions changing jobs

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code's group health plan requirements so that any preexisting-condition limitation period for a person starting coverage after December 31, 1995 must be reduced by the total time that person was covered under prior group health plans [S2] [S3].
Prior coverage counts only if there was no break in coverage longer than 60 days, and waiting periods for enrollment do not count as such a break; COBRA continuation coverage also counts [S3].

For anyone with prior coverage, plans may not set eligibility, enrollment, or contribution rules based on health status, medical condition, claims experience, receipt of health care, medical history, disability, or evidence of insurability [S2] [S3].
Plan administrators must, on request, provide a certification of how long a current or former member was covered, so the new plan can verify prior coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employer health plans and the insurers that back them would pay claims sooner for people who previously would have sat out a preexisting-condition waiting period, and employers would bear some administrative cost for issuing coverage certifications. Those costs can surface as somewhat higher premiums or benefit costs, shared among employers and plan members.

drawbacks.text: Covering preexisting conditions immediately raises claims costs for plans, which can push premiums and employer benefit costs up for everyone in the plan [S3].

The 60-day rule is unforgiving: a person whose coverage lapses for more than two months between jobs loses all credit for earlier years of coverage, and coverage before January 1, 1996 does not count unless it was under the plan the person was enrolled in at the end of 1995 [S3].

The protections attach only to people with prior group coverage; workers coming from uninsurance or from plans without group coverage get no credit, so the bill leaves the newly hired from outside group coverage exposed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it frees workers with health conditions to change or lose jobs without a new penalty period for conditions they already have, and it stops plans from rejecting or surcharging them for their medical history. The costs are higher claims for plans in the short run and some paperwork, and the design limits — the 60-day break rule and the exclusion of most pre-1996 coverage — mean the protection is partial rather than universal. On balance, a modest, well-aimed consumer protection whose main weakness is that it does not go far enough.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 1995 with bipartisan support, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without any markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Thomas introduced the bill on May 11, 1995, joined by 11 original cosponsors from both parties, including Reps. Stark, Cardin, McDermott, Johnson of Connecticut, McCrery, and Crane [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Health [S1] [S5].

It eventually drew 47 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 27 Republicans, but no further action was ever taken on it; it never left subcommittee, never got a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans and plan sponsors came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, they kept the ability to impose preexisting-condition waiting periods and health-based eligibility rules on workers who arrived from other plans, and workers changing jobs continued to bear the cost of gaps in their own coverage.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing from both parties

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee / Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 11, 1995 and referred it to the Subcommittee on Health on May 15; no markup, vote, or further action was ever taken

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: its 12 original sponsors split roughly evenly between the parties, and its 47 cosponsors were 20 Democrats and 27 Republicans; no member is recorded as opposing it, and the obstacle was committee inaction rather than a recorded vote [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer group health plans
industries.note: Preexisting-condition exclusions and health-based eligibility rules save plans money by denying or delaying coverage for conditions new members already have. The bill requires crediting prior coverage and bars health-status-based eligibility for previously covered people, forcing plans to pay those claims instead [S2] [S3].

Employers would bear some additional claims and administrative cost for certifying prior coverage. But portability also reduces job lock, making it easier for employers to hire experienced workers who would otherwise stay put to keep their coverage [S3].
